Excellencies, five years after the Taliban's military return to power, Afghanistan continues to face profound political, humanitarian, economic, social, and human rights challenges. Despite continued diplomatic engagement through various international mechanisms, a durable, just and inclusive political settlement remains elusive. At the heart of challenges is the place of Afghan women in the future of their country. For five years, Afghan women and girls have faced systematic exclusion from education, employment and public life. Yet, they continue to resist exclusion, sustain communities, support education, defend fundamental rights, and advocate for a different future. The question of Afghanistan cannot be reduced solely to humanitarian concerns or even to the reopening of girls' school, important as these issues are. The challenge is much deeper and requires a comprehensive and holistic approach. Current efforts have yet to establish a tangible and accountable pathway through which the people of Afghanistan can exercise their political will and shape their country's future with dignity. We therefore need to change the way the international community speaks about Afghan women. They must not be viewed only as victims in the need of protection. They are political stakeholders They are leaders and they must participate directly and meaningfully in shaping any future political process concerning Afghanistan. Women's participation cannot be reduced to symbolic representation or parallel consultations disconnected from the main political process. If Afghanistan is to move forward, a legitimate and durable political settlement, women must be at the table where decisions are made. We already have important international legal and political frameworks including Security Council Resolution 1325 and broader Women, Peace and Security agenda, CEDAW and other relevant United Nations resolutions and instruments. The challenge is not only the absence of commitments, it is the gap between those commitments and their implementation. But inclusion alone is also not enough. Afghanistan needs a comprehensive and sustainable political solution. That requires a serious discussion about how justice, accountability, acknowledgement of victims, dialogue and national reconciliation can reinforce one another rather than being treated as competing objectives. That is one of the main reasons we have brought these themes together today. women, peace, justice, national reconciliation because they are inseparable. There can be no credible reconciliation if half of the population is excluded. There can be no sustainable political settlement without justice and accountability and there can be no durable peace if people of Afghanistan themselves do not have a meaningful role in determining the political future of their country. Today we hope to focus not only on what has gone wrong, but also on what a credible path forward could look like. How can Afghan women participate as political actors rather than observers? How can the voices of victims, youth, civil society, and Afghanistan's diverse political, ethnic, and religious communities be reflected in a future political process? How can accountability and national reconciliation be pursued together? And how can the United Nations, member states, and regional partners help create conditions for an inclusive, Afghan-owned, Afghan-led political process? These are among central questions we hope to explore today. For the permanent mission of Afghanistan, one principle remains fundamental. Afghanistan's future must ultimately be determined by its people. The Taliban are not only Afghan stakeholders, nor can they alone represent the diversity and aspirations of the Afghan people. No political arrangement can be sustainable if it is imposed through force, exclusion, or fear. And no international process concerning Afghanistan can be credible if Afghans, particularly women, are excluded from shaping its direction. Our task today is therefore to consider how we can help create the political space, international support, and conditions necessary for Afghans themselves to build a more peaceful, just, inclusive, and legitimate future. I hope today's discussion will help us move in this direction. Thank you again for being with us, and I look forward to a substantive and constructive conversation. And because I work in designing risk and data governance architectures for systems, one reality is very clear that currently ordinary consumer apps are engineered to track, store and sync data by default, which makes them hazardous in restrictive settings. So that's my question on how can we take a technology lens on protecting data if people are using it in a safety scenario? Thank you.
I will give that to Sahar, but later on she will respond. We'll go for one more question, and here we will come to Ambassador Seikel and the youth voice.

Can you hear me? Yeah. Thank you. This is really one of the bluntest discussions that I've been privy to on Afghanistan. I'm on the board of directors of the International Center for Transitional Justice, and I was 34 years with the UN and in six peace operations on the ground, from Namibia to Cambodia to Kosovo to Timor, et cetera. And three comments or three issues, I think, were raised but really weren't I think probed enough given their importance. Ambassador Verveer mentioned the international community. I'd like to go into that on what is the Security Council doing? Why hasn't the mandate changed? Is the international community complicit by acquiescing to the division within the council so it's easier to just let the same mandate go on and on. The former Prime Minister mentioning about the outrage, I just saw six months ago the film of the women's movement that's just been issued on the Iceland process. Where is the outrage? Where is the five years we've had to unify people in the world to express our outrage? There's no comparable situation to the situation of women and girls. So that's another piece. And you're very-- Mr. Rahim's point about where's the framework. I was in Cambodia from the start, and in Timor, in Namibia, where we had these big processes. And they're not dictated by the UN. People came together. It's a national-led voice process. But the UN was there to facilitate it. Where are we with this Afghanistan? And there was the big study done for a year, remember? And that was very controversial. Finally, we've got everyone on board on the council to pass that resolution. Whatever happened to it? Where's the special representative or special envoy that was supposed to be appointed? And where's the outrage that hasn't happened? So those three aspects, the complicity, really, of the Security Council and the international community. I don't include the Human Rights Council and entities like that, but I think we really have to ask, you know, the mandate keeps getting renewed. It's easier to not change the mandate. Why? I mean, where's the outrage? And the women, peace and security expert group of the council, I even ask, does it need to be kicked up a peg? Are the permanent reps, I know the answer, the permanent reps are not involved in those discussions. So a rethink on that part too. So I just wanted to say that really, really struck by these comments. I wish the Council would hear, would have all been here to hear that. Thank you.

Thank you. I will give that to Ambassador Milan later to respond. And I will come to Ambassador Seikel and then the youth voice. And we have one more last intervention there, and I think we can wrap it up. Ambassador Seikel.

Thank you very much. I think what we heard in here, again, we should, we must, it needs to be. But there is very little discussion about what are we going to do. After the passage of five years, the answer is very clear. The Taliban is not the answer to anything. The question shouldn't be who the Taliban are and what they do. The question should be who we are and what we do. And I think very good question was raised there. From the, it's our job, it's the job of the people of Afghanistan, it's the job of the non-Taliban camp to put our acts together. And I think there is a clear interest in the part of the opposition to the Taliban to put their acts together. We've had gatherings, numerous gatherings in different places. I would like to thank the First Lady of Austria for being here, Vienna, has been a facilitator of the talks of the people of Afghanistan about what to do. Facilitation of the international community is the key word. That's our expectation. It's our job to put our vision together, to put our strategy together, to put our alternative political structure together, to put our mechanism of implementation and monitoring together. And our call is upon the international community to please be part of the wider non-Taliban camp and facilitate, especially, especially this building where I served for four years. I think we have to give up with reacting. Every time you put a solution on the table of the UN here, we're just looking at it. We don't show interest. The time has come. I think the Security Council is divided. International community is divided. The entire international system has become wobbly given what's happening around the world, what's happening in the Middle East, what's happening in Ukraine and all that. But I think we leave that to the heavyweights to sort it out. Our call is to put our own acts together, and we're working on that. And we call upon the international community to please facilitate. Thank you.
Thank you, Ambassador Saikal. If Ms. Sakhi has a reflection on that one minute, you can share your thinking. I will give the floor to the youth voice.

Excellencies, distinguished ambassadors, professor, and colleagues, thank you very much for the opportunity to contribute to this important discussion today. My name is Baymurzomunbekov. I am a student at Princeton University, and I'm from Kyrgyz Republic, a country in Central Asia that, like Afghanistan, has experienced periods of political and social transformation. And today, I would like to offer a perspective from the younger generation. When we speak about peace and reconciliation, we often focus on immediate objectives of a peace process, ending violence, reaching political agreements, and establishing institutions capable of maintaining that stability. But I believe we should also ask a long-term question: what kind of political community are we building today for the generation that will inherit it? For young people, peace is not simply an outcome of negotiations. It is the political and social and institutional environment in which our generation will live. That is why meaningful youth participation matters. Young people should not be viewed only as beneficiaries of peacebuilding or as a demographic group to be consulted after major decisions have already been made. We are stakeholders in our political future of our countries. And I believe the same principle applies even more fundamentally to women. Women cannot be treated simply as a beneficiaries of peace, protection, or humanitarian assistance. They are political actors whose participation is essential to building a lasting and inclusive peace. For Afghanistan, in particular, this means ensuring that Afghan women are able to participate in discussions about governance, justice, reconciliation, and the future of their country. A peace process cannot be truly inclusive if a significant part of society is absent from the decisions that will define the country's future. And for young people, participation also carries an important responsibility. We are not simply only the generation that will live with the consequences of today's political decisions. We can also contribute to the rebuilding trust, straightening communities, and creating greater understanding across generations. And ultimately, sustainable peace is about more than ending violence. It is about rebuilding trust, creating inclusive institutions, and giving different part of society a place in the country's political life. For Afghanistan, ensuring the meaningful participation of women and young people can therefore be an important part of national healing and reconciliation. Thank you.

Thank you. Thank you for the youth voice from the region and really helping us to once again reflect and the incredible role that youth plays and the peace processes. We have one more intervention and then we will give the floor to speakers, if Mr. Fayek allows me, for one minute reflection to each of these interventions and questions. Please, the floor is yours.

Thank you very much, Ambassador Ross. My name is Ogailo Zawardak, I would say, good evening, everyone. And for my introduction, I am a woman who spent 24 years of her life back in Afghanistan. I've seen my father and my mother both struggle with life in Afghanistan. And that's why I cannot just say, it's unfair for me to say that my mother was the one only struggling. I've seen my father struggle as much in the system, if not more or less than my mother. And that's why my objection to today's discussion is we have left a huge proportion or a huge portion of the society, and that is the rest of the 20 million Afghans, the men in the society. And my question to all of the panelists and people who are participants in here is that what is our plan to, as Mr. Rahim would put it, to galvanize, galvanize and move the rest of the population to actually sustain the progress that was made. And let us ask us one question. What was the reason that we couldn't actually sustain the progress, the developments that were made between 2001 and 2021? What is the reason? And also I would ask a question. If the international community has failed to encourage the people of Afghanistan to stand on their own feet and put their act together, and I would say yes, they have failed, because I would ask how long will we rely on outsiders to make us recognize our rights for women, because at the end of the day, women are supposed to live with their husbands, their fathers, their brothers, and that's part of their daily life. They cannot leave their homes. And if those people who are living with them at their homes are not able to protect them, do not have that courage to protect them, then I think we failed as a community to make that change as the international community. And for me, my goal, my vision for an Afghanistan, a successful, an ideal Afghanistan as a woman would be for my father to live as prosperous as my mother, my brother to have the same opportunities as me. And as Mr. Rahim put it, the boys are not doing as well. They are getting subpar education too. I'm not here to speak for boys, but what I'm saying is that We should think of moving the men. We should actually think of how to reason with them, how to bring them to the table, how to make them recognize what the women in Afghanistan has suffered and has been suffering. And there should be a way. I don't accept the reason that there isn't any way to speak and reason with them. I've spoken to men, I've spoken to my father, and I know, I know there is a way. And we should stop alienating them. We should stop and eliminating them from the discussion. Thank you. And I would appreciate to hear more about how to move them around, how to encourage them to help and support the women.

Thank you. Thank you. Thank you so much. I will let that to Ms. Mehran to respond in one minute. So we can start with Ms. Mehran and then Raheem Seib and then Farishta John. Ms. Alukozei and Ambassador Milan. We will give you the hardest part to sort of wrap that up.

So I have maybe 60 seconds and I divided. Let me see if I can take care of it. First, on the complicity issue, we have also raised this question of UNAMA and also the larger UN bodies inside Afghanistan, are they complicit in violation of the UN Charter and its principles? Because it's been a year that women of Afghanistan are not allowed within the UN premises, as the various think. There is ban on female aid workers. me and my legal colleagues, we are thinking about an assessment that has been done in Myanmar to see if we can put that ask forward that something like that can happen in Afghanistan or something, because there is a case. I'm not sure if I can clearly speak on legality of it, but this is concern of complicity is something that women of Afghanistan and the movement of women and also men have been raising it. So, yes, we are thinking about it. And on the main issue, so when we speak about gender apartheid, how we are analyzing and studying the situation in Afghanistan is how it's part of the governing strategy of the Taliban. And that's where we see the women and men are coerced into enforcement of those policies. on a lot of these bans and laws, men are subject to punishment too. And then if you see madrasification process of the Taliban to socially engineer the society in a way that can, the regime of the Taliban can sustain. So you see women are subject, men are equally being violated in the process. And that's what we are discussing and hopefully the implication on the larger society is seen by men, too, and men who speak on behalf of women and come on the streets and raise, they are being imprisoned and tortured. So that is part of the discussion of codification of gender apartheid, too, on how men are coerced into implementing those decrees. And we can talk more about it if you need it further clarification.

Thank you. I would quickly Yes, I know. I'll quickly go to the question. Thank you very much for asking me this question. This was part of the panel discussion, but you couldn't ask it. So what I would suggest is that not only this group, but broader group, and as Ambassador Saikal said, the UN should lead to bring the Afghan women from being the agenda point for discussion and turning them into a voice that discuss Afghanistan. Let's stop discussing Afghan women. Help them start talking about Afghanistan themselves. Isn't it possible to give a seat to the Afghan women at the General Assembly every year? We have the women forums, women NGOs. We can have an election, which again will demonstrate the political activism among the Afghan women and then bring them into the General Assembly, to the Security Council, so that they don't talk about Afghan women, as you said, but they talk about Afghanistan and the broader issue of Afghanistan. That is men, women, Afghan society. I begin my talk about Afghan society, so yes, That's the bare minimum that international community can do. And the facilitation, as you talked about, is the bare minimum that is the responsibility of the United Nations that it should be undertaking. Thank you.

Continuation of what Ambassador Serkel mentioned. I strongly recommend that when Afghans are sitting around the table to provide a vision for peace, It should include accountability and reconciliation at the heart of it, because any peace process that lacks accountability and reconciliation as key factors, it will kind of slide back to chaos. And when we talk about accountability, we have to understand that we are a country in fragility and conflict for the last for decades. So there is a lot of accumulated grievances, accumulated trauma, and a lot of violations of women human rights that should be taken into consideration. And all stages of conflict should be assessed, and based on that, an inclusive peace process with these two components should be taken into account. Thank you.

About technology being used as means to provide education, that is a method that we see prominently in Afghanistan's education interventions right now. However, by no means can these online educational methods or models that are being introduced be a replacement for a formal national education system in the country. It is a great immediate intervention to be introduced, but it comes with its own set of challenges. Safety is one of them, but other challenges that comes with it is access to the internet. How many Afghan women have access to Internet, how many of them have access to devices to be able to attend these programs. We do have an online program at Sahar and that is the most challenging program we have had so far, even more challenging than the in-person underground programs that we are running right now because of those--because these challenges are so out of control that we can't have solutions to immediately. And I also wanted to quickly comment on men inclusion of men in these discussions. I highly, highly support that and one way could be introducing programs that are working with younger men to disrupt that cycle before it translates into their adulthood. We are running a similar program at Sahar. We name it Men as Partners in Change and we look at women's issue from a male perspective and how men can support women and their families and communities to reach their full potential. But yes, that's an important aspect of the work that we all should be doing. Thank you.

Just really quickly, particularly to follow up on Nina Lahood's point about the Security Council. I think we need accountability in the Security Council because really when the process for Afghanistan was adopted a couple of years ago, not just the Secretary General's representative, but also that mosaic process that has faltered in terms of being a comprehensive process, the independent, all kinds of things. And the whole point of it was we need a strategic plan in the Security Council for Afghanistan, and that's been missing. So I endorse what you said, and I hope we can find a way to put more pressure on. I think it is political and lack of attention or concern. And I just want to respond really quickly to what you said, because I think for society to come together, it has to be men and women. And it's not a zero sum game. When women benefit, men benefit. When men benefit, women should benefit. I worry about the madrasa education of young men today that's happening in Afghanistan. Very extreme interpretation. It's going to affect this. thinking that you mentioned is problematic potentially for the future. If that's the only way the boys of Afghanistan are gonna learn, that's not a good outcome for the future of the country.
